title: m-pseudo-coherence in ringed-site distinguished triangles
statement: Let $(\mathcal C,\mathcal O)$ be a site with a sheaf of commutative rings and use its unbounded derived category of module sheaves [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category, def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. Restrictions to an object mean restrictions to the slice site [def-pur-localized-ringed-site]. A strictly perfect complex is a bounded cochain complex whose terms are direct summands of finite free $\mathcal O$-modules. For $a\in\mathbf Z$, call $K\in D(\mathcal O)$ $a$-pseudo-coherent if locally on each site object there is a strictly perfect $P$ and a morphism $P\to K$ inducing cohomology isomorphisms in degrees $>a$ and a surjection in degree $a$. Let $m\in\mathbf Z$ and let $K\to L\to M\to K[1]$ be a distinguished triangle in $D(\mathcal O)$. (1) If $K$ is $(m+1)$-pseudo-coherent and $L$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent, then $M$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent. (2) If $K$ and $M$ are $m$-pseudo-coherent, then $L$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent. (3) If $L$ is $(m+1)$-pseudo-coherent and $M$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent, then $K$ is $(m+1)$-pseudo-coherent.

proof.text: Fix an object $U$. Restriction of module sheaves to any slice is exact; applying it degreewise gives a triangulated restriction on derived categories and commutes with cohomology. Thus the given triangle restricts to every further slice. For (1), choose a covering of $U$ with strictly perfect approximations $\alpha:P\to K$ at degree $m+1$. On each member choose a covering carrying a strictly perfect approximation $\beta:Q\to L$ at degree $m$. We work on a member of this composite covering and suppress restrictions. Further restrictions preserve these properties: finite free sheaves and their retracts restrict to finite free sheaves and their retracts, and exact restriction preserves the cohomology isomorphisms and epimorphisms.

Replace $P$ by its stupid truncation $P'=\sigma_{\ge m+1}P$: it has the same terms and differentials from degree $m+1$ onwards and zero terms below. The canonical inclusion $P'\to P$ is a chain map, is an isomorphism on cohomology above $m+1$, and is surjective in degree $m+1$, since it removes the incoming boundaries in that degree without changing cycles. Hence $\alpha':P'\to K$ still has exactly the required approximation properties. Its terms are unchanged or zero, so $P'$ remains strictly perfect and is zero below $m+1$.

Choose any cochain representative $F$ of $L$. Apply the local-actual lemma to $\beta:Q\to L\cong Q(F)$ and then to $f\alpha':P'\to L\cong Q(F)$; refine the covering to obtain actual chain maps $b:Q\to F$ and $c:P'\to F$ representing these two arrows. The chain map $b$ is an isomorphism on cohomology above $m$ and a surjection at $m$. Apply the local homotopy-lifting lemma to $E=P'$, $G=Q$, $u=c$, $v=b$, and $a=m+1$. Its support condition holds by the previous step, and $H^j(b)$ is an isomorphism for every $j\ge m+1$, hence in particular surjective at $a$. After one more covering it gives a chain map $\gamma:P'\to Q$ with $b\gamma$ homotopic to $c$. Localization identifies homotopic maps, so $\beta\,Q(\gamma)=f\alpha'$ in the derived category. This supplies the actual chain map omitted in the source's diagram argument, without imposing global projectivity on sheaves.

Put $C=\operatorname{Cone}(\gamma)$. Its degree-$j$ term is $Q^j\oplus P'^{j+1}$, so it is zero outside a finite interval; the direct sum of two finite-free retracts is a retract of the direct sum of their finite free ambient modules. Thus $C$ is strictly perfect, directly from the cone formula. The image of the cone triangle $P'\to Q\to C\to P'[1]$ is distinguished. TR3 applied to the commutative square from the previous step completes $(\alpha',\beta)$ to a morphism of this triangle into $K\to L\to M\to K[1]$; denote its third component by $\theta:Q(C)\to M$.

Apply the long exact cohomology sequence and its naturality for morphisms of triangles. For $j>m$, use the five-term rows $H^j(P')\to H^j(Q)\to H^j(C)\to H^{j+1}(P')\to H^{j+1}(Q)$ and $H^j(K)\to H^j(L)\to H^j(M)\to H^{j+1}(K)\to H^{j+1}(L)$. The first vertical arrow is epic (including $j=m+1$); the second and fourth are isomorphisms and the fifth is monic. The five lemma makes $H^j(\theta)$ an isomorphism. At degree $m$ use instead the four-term rows $H^m(Q)\to H^m(C)\to H^{m+1}(P')\to H^{m+1}(Q)$ and their target row. The first and third vertical arrows are epic and the fourth monic. The epi four lemma therefore makes the second vertical arrow $H^m(\theta)$ epic. All assertions take place in the abelian category of module sheaves, not in section groups.

We have constructed on a covering of every initially arbitrary $U$ a strictly perfect $C$ and a map to $M$ which is a cohomology isomorphism above $m$ and an epimorphism at $m$. The successive coverings used above compose to a covering by the site axiom; slice coverings and relocalization are precisely those in the localized-site definition. This is exactly the stated local approximation definition of $m$-pseudo-coherence, proving (1).

For any integer $r$, shifting a strictly perfect approximation and shifting it back shows directly that $X[r]$ is $a$-pseudo-coherent if and only if $X$ is $(a+r)$-pseudo-coherent: the terms are reindexed with sign $(-1)^r$ on the differential, $H^j(X[r])=H^{j+r}(X)$, and the same holds for the approximation map. For (2), inverse rotation gives the distinguished triangle $M[-1]\to K\to L\to M$. Since $M$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent, $M[-1]$ is $(m+1)$-pseudo-coherent; apply the already proved (1) with middle term $K$ to deduce that $L$ is $m$-pseudo-coherent. For (3), rotation gives $L\to M\to K[1]\to L[1]$. Apply (1) to get $K[1]$ $m$-pseudo-coherent, hence $K$ $(m+1)$-pseudo-coherent by the same shift calculation. The rotation signs do not change any cohomology isomorphism or epimorphism.
